nameStory: The Labrador Thin-legged Wolf Spider gets its name from where it was first scientifically described - the rugged Labrador region of eastern Canada. Like other thin-legged wolf spiders, it has notably slender, delicate-looking legs compared to its bulkier wolf spider cousins. The 'wolf' part comes from these spiders' hunting style - they don't build webs to catch prey, but instead roam and pounce on victims like tiny wolves.
description: The Labrador Thin-legged Wolf Spider is a small, ground-dwelling hunter that prowls New England's northern landscapes. These compact spiders typically measure about 6-8 millimeters in body length, with females slightly larger than males. They have the characteristic wolf spider build - a robust front section (cephalothorax) and rounded abdomen - but their legs are notably thinner and more delicate than most wolf spiders. Their coloration tends toward muted browns and grays with subtle patterns that help them blend into rocky and sandy environments.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large eyes arranged in a square on top of the head, with four smaller eyes below - shine a flashlight at night and they'll reflect back like tiny green diamonds

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, sturdy build with a slightly flattened appearance when viewed from above, feeling firm but not hard if gently touched

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Muted brown and gray coloration with subtle darker stripes or chevron patterns on the abdomen that may be barely visible in dim light

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small for a wolf spider at 6-8mm body length - about the size of a pencil eraser, with legs that don't feel as thick or strong as larger wolf spiders

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Active hunter that runs in quick bursts across open ground, often freezing motionless when disturbed before darting to cover

habitat: Look for Labrador Thin-legged Wolf Spiders in New England's northern and mountainous regions, particularly in rocky areas with sparse vegetation. They favor well-drained sandy or gravelly soils around stone outcrops, alpine meadows, and exposed ridgelines. These spiders seem to prefer cooler microclimates and are most likely found in areas that stay relatively cool even during summer months.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter shelters under rocks and begin hunting as temperatures warm, though they may still be sluggish on cool mornings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible hunting during daylight hours and mating occurs, with females carrying distinctive round egg sacs.
seasonality.fall: Spiderlings disperse and adults prepare for winter, often seen basking on sun-warmed rocks during the day to absorb heat.
seasonality.winter: Hidden under rocks, logs, or in crevices in a dormant state, occasionally emerging on unusually warm winter days.

funFact: Despite being called 'thin-legged,' these spiders can actually support and carry an egg sac that's nearly as large as their own body, running around with it attached to their spinnerets like a soccer ball - and if the egg sac gets damaged, the mother will carefully repair it with fresh silk.
confusionNotes: With only two recorded observations in New England, this species is easily confused with other thin-legged wolf spiders, especially the more common Shore Spider and Ubiquitous Thin-legged Wolf Spider. The key memory trick: Labrador spiders prefer cool, rocky northern habitats rather than the warmer, sandy areas favored by their cousins.
contextualKnowledge: The extremely low observation count (only 2 recorded sightings in New England) suggests this species may be at the very southern edge of its range here, making any sighting particularly noteworthy for regional biodiversity records.
compareHints: Among the thin-legged wolf spiders in New England, the Labrador species tends to be found in the coolest, most northern habitats compared to relatives like the Shore Spider (which prefers beaches and lakeshores) or the Ubiquitous Thin-legged Wolf Spider (found in warmer, more diverse habitats). The Labrador species' preference for rocky, alpine-like conditions sets it apart from most of its genus-mates. Its markings are typically more subdued and grayish compared to the often warmer brown tones of related species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the thin-legged wolf spiders in its genus, the Stone Spider stands out for its exclusive coastal habitat preference and darker coloration.

Among the thin-legged wolf spiders in New England, the Shiny Wolf Spider is distinguished by its notably glossy appearance - the Shore Spider and Stone Spider tend to be more matte, while the Saltmarsh species is typically found in coastal areas rather than inland forests.

Among its Pardosa relatives, the Shore Spider is distinguished primarily by its strong preference for waterside habitats - while the Stone Spider prefers rocky areas and the Saltmarsh Thin-legged Wolf Spider sticks to coastal salt marshes.
Among the many Pardosa species in New England, this is the only one restricted to saltmarsh habitats.

Among its Pardosa relatives, the Pale Thin-legged Wolf Spider is distinguished by its lighter overall coloration compared to the darker Shiny Wolf Spider, and its preference for drier habitats unlike the Shore Spider which stays near water.

Compared to its Pardosa relatives in New England, saxatilis tends to be more strictly associated with rocky habitats than species like the Shore Spider (found in sandy areas) or Shiny Wolf Spider (found in various ground habitats).

Among the ten Pardosa species in New England, the Little Banded Wolf Spider is distinguished by its leg banding - most relatives like the Shiny Wolf Spider or Shore Spider have plain legs without distinct bands.

Among New England's thin-legged wolf spiders, the Ubiquitous Thin-legged Wolf Spider lacks the distinct habitat preferences of its relatives - it's not tied to shores like the Shore Spider or saltmarshes like the Saltmarsh Thin-legged Wolf Spider.
Pardosa pauxilla is distinguished from its Pardosa relatives primarily by its very small size.
Pardosa luteola is distinguished from other thin-legged wolf spiders in New England primarily by its yellowish coloration and coastal/sandy habitat preferences.
